articles.title: Lost Grounds: Football's most iconic former stadiums
articles.summary: Lost Grounds: Footballs most iconic former stadiums
articles.body:
Football grounds are not just where the game is played but where it is remembered. They are the places where generations return to the same turnstiles, climb the same steps and take their place in the same stands. They become landmarks in their own right — woven into the identity of a club and the neighbourhood around it. But football is always changing. Stands and terraces have been demolished beneath new developments. Clubs have moved across towns and cities. Where thousands once gathered on a Saturday afternoon, there may now be a supermarket, a housing estate or nothing at all. Yet a football ground rarely disappears completely. Its name survives in old photographs. Its outline remains faintly visible in the streets around it. Supporters remember where they stood, where they celebrated, where they watched their team win — and where they said goodbye. These are the stories of football's lost grounds: the iconic stadiums that once formed the backdrop to the game, and the traces they left behind.

Manchester City played at Maine Road for 80 years before moving to the City of Manchester Stadium built for the 2002 Commonwealth Games.

Maine Road had a capacity of 35,150 but its record attendance was more than double that when 84,569 supporters watched their FA Cup sixth-round tie against Stoke in 1934.

Man City beat Man Utd in the final Manchester derby at Maine Road with help from a mistake by Gary Neville.

Maine Road was demolished in 2003 and is now a housing estate with a circular plate symbolising the centre spot.

Bolton Wanderers played at Burnden Park for 102 years before moving to the Reebok Stadium in 1997.

One of the most iconic aspects of the ground was the railway track where trains would run behind the stand and it was captured in the 1955 film The Love Match .

Burnden Park was also the scene of one of the worst tragedies in British football history when 33 Bolton fans were crushed to death and another 400 injured during an FA Cup quarter-final second-leg tie against Stoke City in 1946.

There was estimated to be a crowd of 85,000 at the game, which was at least 15,000 more than the ground's capacity.

The stadium was demolished in 1999, two years after Bolton moved out, and is now a supermarket.

Roker Park was Sunderland's home for 99 years before the club moved to the Stadium of Light.

The 'Roker Roar' was said to be able to be heard five miles away.

The ground's capacity was originally designed to accommodate a crowd of 60,000.

Its capacity was gradually reduced to around 22,500. Roker Park's record attendance was 75,188 for Sunderland's FA Cup tie against Derby in 1933. 75,118.

During the 1966 World Cup, Roker Park hosted three group stage games and the quarter-final between the Soviet Union and Hungary.

England's men's team also played there on three occasions plus one England women's match.

Roker Park is now a housing estate with the roads named Midfield Drive, Roker Park Close, Promotion Close and Clockstand Close.

Stoke City played at the Victoria Ground for 199 years.

When they left in 1997, it was the oldest operational stadium in English football.

The Victoria Ground was home to some of English football's greats such as Sir Stanley Matthews and Gordon Banks.

The site lay derelict for 20 years before it was redeveloped into a housing estate.

Frank Soo Street sits among the houses in honour of the former Stoke player who made more than 250 appearances for the club, was the first person of Asian heritage to appear in the Football League and the first to represent England.

Soo, whose father was Chinese, played in nine England wartime matches between 1942 and 1945.

Located on the banks of the River Severn, Shrewsbury Town began playing at Gay Meadow in September 1910 and, only a few months later, a match was abandoned for the first time due to flooding - a sign of things to come!

Shrewsbury fan Fred Davies became a legandary figure at the club for his unique role as a ball boy. He would board a coracle and paddle into the river to collect stray footballs, as demonstrated by Sky Sports News' Ben Ransom!

Shrewsbury moved into the New Meadow, a 10,000-seat stadium, in 2007. Gay Meadow was converted into flats.

Ayresome Park was Middlesbrough's home for 92 years, between 1903 and 1995, before they moved to the Riverside Stadium. It was the venue for one of the biggest shocks in World Cup history, when North Korea beat Italy 1-0 in July 1966, courtesy of a goal from Pak Doo-ik. Members of the North Korea squad returned to Teesside in 2002 after a bronze casting of a football boot imprint was unveiled to mark the spot on the housing estate where the goal was scored. It was declared a national monument of the nation. The gates of Ayresome Park have since been erected outside the main entrance of the Riverside.

Millmoor was first home to Rotherham County from 1907 to 1925, then, when they merged with Rotherham Town, it was Rotherham United from 1925 until 2008. The Millers moved on to the Don Valley Stadium in Sheffield, then the New York Stadium, but Millmoor continued to stand. For the best part of the last 10 years, football continued to be played at the stadium, but demolition began in the summer and is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

Filbert Street was Leicester's home for more than 100 years and hosted its last match in May 2002, before the Foxes made the move to the Walkers Stadium - now the King Power - just a stone's throw away.

Within 12 months, the stadium was razed to the ground and, on part of the site, student accommodation was built, as well as a new road named after Leicester legend Gary Lineker.

Until recently, the rest was left as wasteland, and there is little to mark its former history, but work is now under way to build housing on the remaining land.

Brentford had five temporary homes before they moved into Griffin Park - built on the site of a former orchard - in 1904.

It became well-known for the uniqueness of having a pub on every corner: The Griffin, The Princess Royal, The New Inn and The Royal Oak.

One of the most memorable days came in April 2013, when forward Marcello Trotta hit the crossbar with a last-minute penalty that, had it been scored, would have sent Brentford into the Championship.

The final match in front of fans was the 5-0 win over Sheffield Wednesday in March 2020, with the last first-team game a 3-1 win over Swansea in the Championship play-offs just under five months later.

Griffin Park has since been demolished and the site is currently flat, though there are plans to build new homes in the near future.

Arsenal only arrived in north London in 1913. The club had been based at the Manor Ground in Plumstead, south-east London.

Chairman Henry Norris believed they needed a more prosperous location and a larger potential supporter base. Highbury's proximity to the Underground was a major attraction.

The move was controversial with Tottenham Hotspur and Clapton Orient objecting to Arsenal establishing themselves so close.

The famous Clock End was introduced by Herbert Chapman in the 1930s. It originally provided a 45-minute countdown, but the FA objected because it could undermine the match officials' authority, so it was changed to a conventional clock.

Highbury eventually accommodated more than 70,000 spectators before becoming an all-seater stadium. By the time Arsenal left in 2006, capacity was around 38,000.

Arsenal won their first league title there in 1931, then nine more before leaving, including the famous 2003/04 Invincibles season.

Highbury is now a private garden surrounded by Highbury Square, a residential development of more than 650 apartments.

Arsenal announced plans to leave Highbury in 1999, with Ashburton Grove - less than half a mile away - chosen for the new Emirates Stadium offering 60,000 seats.

In 2004, Arsene Wenger, Thierry Henry and Patrick Vieira were among those involved in placing a capsule at the new stadium containing memorabilia and keepsakes from Highbury

The Taylor Report - which came from the inquiry into the 1989 Hillsborough disaster - ruled that major stadiums were required to become all-seater by the summer of 1994.

Wimbledon's board decided that was not a viable option for Plough Lane, so the Dons shared Selhurst Park with Crystal Palace from 1991 to 2003. The two clubs' reserve teams played at the stadium until 1998.

They never returned home, though, and were instead controversially reformed as MK Dons from the 2003/04 season onwards. Plough Lane was demolished in 2002 and a housing development was completed in 2008.

However, the 'new' Plough Lane Stadium, built just 200 yards from the old one, was completed in 2020 and has been the home of AFC Wimbledon ever since.

White Hart Lane started life as a nursery. Spurs moved to the site in 1899, when it was a disused market garden owned by the Charrington brewery. Greenhouses and even remnants of the old nursery were still discovered during pitch work in 1952.

It wasn't originally called White Hart Lane. The ground was initially called the High Road ground or White Hart grounds.

White Hart Lane's record league crowd was 70,882 against Manchester United in 1951. The ground's eventual capcity was 36,000.

The Tottenham Hotspur Stadium opened in April 2019 and has a capacity of 62,850, making it the third-largest ground in England.

The £1bn ground has become the benchmark for modern stadia and occupies the same site as White Hart Lane meaning the club has effectively been playing football here since 1899 — more than 125 years.

The South Stand holds 17,500, making it the largest single-tier stand in the UK. The famous golden cockerel, around for more than a century, sits above it.

The stadium was designed to be much more than a football ground. Its retractable pitch can divide into sections, allowing the venue to host NFL, concerts, boxing and rugby as well as Spurs matches.

The original Wembley Stadium was opened in April 1923, when Bolton beat West Ham 2-0 in the FA Cup final in front of a crowd of 126,047 - a record that was never beaten.

England played their first match there 16 days short of a year later, drawing 1-1 with Scotland and in 1966 won the World Cup for the first and only time so far, beating West Germany 4-2, thanks to Geoff Hurst's famous hat-trick.

Their final appearance there came in October 2000, when Dietmar Hamann sealed a 1-0 win for Germany, which preceded Kevin Keegan's resignation as manager.

Wembley's famous Twin Towers were given Grade II listed status in the mid-1970s, but demolished in 2003 in preparation for the construction of the 'new' Wembley, which opened in 2007.

Southampton moved to The Dell in 1898, 15 years after they were founded, but started to put plans in place for a new stadium in the wake of the Taylor Report. Requirements for top-level stadiums to become all-seater meant the capacity was reduced to just 15,200 - the lowest in the Premier League. The move to St Mary's was announced in the summer of 1999 and construction began later that year. The 2000/01 season was the club's last at The Dell, and they said farewell in perfect fashion, by coming back from 1-0 down to beat Arsenal 3-2, with club legend Matt Le Tissier scoring the winner. Saints made the move a couple of miles down the road to their new home at the start of 2001/02, by which time The Dell had been demolished. A housing estate was built on the site, with, the former centre circle marked by a garden in the middle of the development.

The Goldstone Ground was Brighton's home for 95 years until the club sold the freehold to clear debts, despite having arranged no alternative home ground and facing protests from supporters. The final match at the ground was a crucial 1-0 victory over Doncaster Rovers, which moved Brighton off the bottom of the Division Three table before a draw at Hereford on the final day kept them up.

The site was redeveloped into a retail park.

Brighton initially groundshared at Gillingham, over 70 miles away, before returning to Hove at the Withdean athletics stadium in 1999.

Brighton spent over 10 seasons there, rising to the Championship while a new stadium in Falmer eventually achieved planning permission and was built.

The Boleyn Ground, also known as Upton Park, was West Ham United's home in East London until it was demolished for housing, with the club moving to the London Stadium in Stratford.

Sir Bobby Moore, Sir Geoff Hurst and Martin Peters, England World Cup winners in 1966, all played for West Ham at the time and are immortalised with a bronze statue outside Upton Park.

The 35,000-capacity stadium witnessed a dramatic 3-2 victory over Manchester United in its final game in 2016.

Moving to the Olympic Stadium wasn't popular among many West Ham supporters and it has proved to be a difficult transition both emotionally and physically.

The club were unable to consistently improve in the Premier League and have since been relegated to the Championship.

London Stadium LLP runs the stadium and is owned by the Greater London Authority, so its losses of £19m a year are ultimately met by taxpayers.

The stadium, rather than the club, covers the costs of stewarding, policing and pitch maintenance. West Ham pay up to £2.5m a year in rent under its 99-year deal, signed in 2013.

articles.title: How Keith Alexander blazed a trail for black football managers
articles.summary: Ex-players and family members on the legacy of the late Lincoln, Peterborough and Macclesfield boss.
articles.body:
When Keith Alexander died in 2010, he was honoured up and down the country, including on one of football's biggest stages as England players donned black armbands for a match at Wembley.

It was a fitting tribute to a man who was not only an admired and respected figure in the game, but a trailblazer who helped pave the way for more black managers in English professional football.

As part of Black History Month , those who knew him best have been reflecting on his lasting impact.

"Keith remains a beacon of hope for us all, and I know his story continues to inspire us," says Leon Mann, a co-founder of the Football Black List , which gives out an award in his memory.

"When we see a number of black British or black managers in the Premier League, we should pause and remember Keith's contribution, because it would have played its part, one hundred per cent."

Although he was not the first permanent black manager in the Football League – Tony Collins took the reins at Rochdale in 1960 – Alexander helped inspire a new generation to follow in his footsteps after spells in charge of Lincoln City, Peterborough United and Macclesfield, among others.

Born in Nottingham in 1956 to St Lucian parents, Alexander was proud of his English upbringing and Caribbean heritage, his sons Matt and Paul say.

Alexander spoke openly about the racism he encountered as a player, which included monkey chants and bananas being thrown at him.

"He experienced loads of it, especially in his early days," Matt says. "There was loads of racism and throwing bananas, that kind of stuff.

"I'd be really surprised if you spoke to any black footballer of that generation who hadn't experienced the same sort of thing."

Despite this, Paul says race was rarely discussed at home.

"It was never a conversation about how difficult it was for black youths growing up.

"It was, you will be successful at what you do and you work hard for what you want."

However, he adds: "I think he was conscious he did have to work twice as hard."

After a long playing career, Alexander took charge of Lincoln City in 1993. After a season in charge, he went on to manage non-league Ilkeston Town and Northwich Victoria.

In 2002, he was named Lincoln boss for a second spell and, working with a tight budget, helped guide the club from the depths of administration to the League Two play-off places in four successive seasons.

Former striker Franny Green says Alexander will always be remembered for "bringing players from non-league and giving them an opportunity".

"If you go through Lincoln's history, Keith's name is going to be one of the biggest when it comes to what he did."

Green recalls having a real affinity with Alexander. "I think it helped because of my race and Keith's race," he adds.

Recalling the first time he met Alexander during a trial at Ilkeston, Green says: "I was 16, this tall slim kid with a mini afro and he was just really charming towards me.

"He said just go and play football – there's no pressure."

Simon Weaver joined Lincoln City in the summer of 2002 after previously playing under Alexander at Ilkeston.

He recalls his former boss's great ability to unite a dressing room.

One moment that sticks in his memory is the first time he was invited for a training session at Ilkeston.

"I played quite well in training – afterwards I went and knocked on his [office] and he was sat there with his feet up and a bunch of grapes."

Weaver was asked to "just come and play" for the team on Saturday.

"He was just so relaxed," he recalls. "He just made me feel at ease, saying just come and do you what you did [in training].

"We played away first game and won – I got a black eye and I'm thinking, 'I'm liking this, this is my cup of tea'."

Alexander was managing Macclesfield when he died in 2010 after falling ill after a game . He was 53.

Tributes poured in from across football , with clubs across the country observing a minute's silence.

At the time, his son Paul described him as "a very humble man", adding: "He didn't realise the impact he had on others just by walking into a room."

In recent years, players who have received the Keith Alexander Award from the Football Black List have included Yaya Toure, Shaka Hislop and Kerry Davis, the first black woman to play for the England women's national team.

His legacy also lives on through the Sacred Sports Foundation, which he founded in St Lucia to help young people through sport.

Mann, of the Football Black List, says Alexander will be remembered for the opportunities he created for others and his willingness to challenge racism in football – and that should never be forgotten.

CORRECTION, 5 October 2026: An earlier version of this article suggested Alexander died after falling ill at a game. He actually fell ill at home after the game.

articles.title: Roberto Gómez alerta tras el 7-0 del Barcelona: "Florentino Pérez puede hartarse del Madrid femenino"
articles.standfirst: El periodista considera que una goleada así "desmotiva a los aficionados" y advierte de las posibles consecuencias para el proyecto femenino del conjunto blanco
articles.summary: El periodista considera que una goleada así "desmotiva a los aficionados" y advierte de las posibles consecuencias para el proyecto femenino del conjunto blanco
articles.body: Roberto Gómez analizó en La Tribu de Radio MARCA la contundente victoria del Barcelona frente al Real Madrid en el Clásico femenino. Desde el aeropuerto de Miami y volviendo a España tras el X Torneo Internacional LALIGA FC FUTURES Orlando 2026, el periodista se mostró muy crítico con lo sucedido y alertó de las consecuencias que, a su juicio, puede tener una diferencia tan amplia entre ambos equipos. "La victoria apabullante del Barcelona frente al Real Madrid me parece una vergüenza. Esto, desde luego, desmotiva a los aficionados, desmotiva a los jugadores", aseguró Roberto Gómez. El periodista reconoció la superioridad azulgrana, pero considera que una derrota de estas dimensiones podría afectar al futuro del proyecto madridista: "Es cierto que lo normal es que el Barcelona es un equipo superior, pero esta humillación puede tener dos salidas". Roberto Gómez puso sobre la mesa uno de los escenarios que, en su opinión, podría provocar este resultado: "Que Florentino Pérez se harte de la sección y corte, indudablemente, la trayectoria, que por otra parte está siendo en los últimos tiempos bastante correcta, del equipo de mujeres del conjunto madridista". La otra posibilidad, según explicó, sería que el Real Madrid decidiera continuar por el mismo camino. Gómez volvió a reconocer la enorme dimensión del conjunto azulgrana: "Más allá de la actitud deportiva, de la superioridad del Barça, que es probablemente el mejor equipo del mundo y de la historia, hay un poco de venganza, hay un poco de pique y hay un poco bastante de mala leche". Para el periodista, esta situación termina perjudicando a la propia competición: "Esto es muy malo para la competición". Durante su intervención, Roberto Gómez también adelantó posibles novedades relacionadas con el arbitraje, aunque sin entrar en detalles: "Atención, tendremos noticias importantes del mundo del arbitraje. Y aquí lo dejo". Además, defendió la labor de Fran Soto: "Hay que apoyar ahora más que nunca al presidente del colectivo arbitral. Está teniendo desde luego mucho trabajo y lo está resolviendo hasta el momento muy bien". Y terminó dejando otro aviso de cara al futuro: "Los árbitros tienen que estar a su altura, pero hablaremos, y me da la impresión que muy bien, próximamente de Fran Soto".

articles.title: Morgan Rogers: Why £117m Chelsea star failed at Bournemouth
articles.summary: A look at the point in club-record £117m Chelsea signing Morgan Rogers' career when he doubted whether he could make it at the highest level.
articles.body:
Three years before becoming Chelsea 's £117m club-record signing, Morgan Rogers watched his value fall to just £1m and questioned whether he would make it at all.

For Rogers, the transition from academy football to the men's game was not as seamless as he had hoped and, in his own words, it took a series of "difficult loans" for him to break through.

Bournemouth , who Chelsea face at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, were the first of two underwhelming Championship loan spells for Rogers, alongside a later stint at Blackpool, while he was a Manchester City player.

It was a setback for a player who had been a regular England youth international and one of West Bromwich Albion's brightest academy prospects.

In a recent interview with Chelsea 's club channel, Rogers said that period taught him how to "take knocks".

Asked what his rise through the EFL had taught him, he replied: "Everything."

After a long pause, he added: "I needed that next challenge, to be taken out of my comfort zone and find the player I was going to be in professional football.

"I think the academy player I was, if you watch me then, is not the same player I am now. I am a completely different player. I had to learn that on loan.

"The one thing I learned when going through these difficult loans is that I couldn't care less what people say about me. I just care about what I can control."

"I don't think there's such a thing as a bad loan," Rogers' first loan manager at Lincoln City, Michael Appleton, told BBC Sport.

Appleton had worked in West Brom's academy and knew Rogers was one of the most highly rated prospects there. He made it his mission to bring him to Sincil Bank in League One.

He remembers Rogers having a big personality and speaking up in team meetings despite arriving as an 18-year-old. The forward went on to score six goals and provide two assists in 28 appearances after joining shortly after lockdown.

En route to the play-off final, which Lincoln lost to Blackpool, Appleton recalls one moment in particular.

"We played Portsmouth away and they had three or four absolute units in the team," he added. "We were setting up for set-pieces and almost running out of players to pick up these giants.

"Without any hesitation whatsoever, Morgan said: 'Make me a marker. I'll head the ball out of our box.'

"He was full of confidence because he was playing well, but he took the defensive side of the game just as seriously as trying to impact the opposition's box. For me, that's a great example of him as a person and as a player."

However, after earning an opportunity in the Championship with Bournemouth , Rogers started only three matches and scored once under then-manager Scott Parker, whose side secured promotion back to the Premier League.

Rogers had little impact and was described as a "slow burner" by former scout Des Taylor, who brought him in.

He added: "You could see his ability having scouted him at Lincoln, but it wasn't clear what he would become. We saw his Lincoln loan spell turn him from a boy into a man.

"He showed he could handle the physical side of things after coming from Man City's academy. Unfortunately, we signed him late in the window. We saw him as a number 10, but Parker was not really playing with a number 10.

"I don't think it was a great time for him because he wasn't getting game time and, when he did, it wasn't in the position he wanted. He was a victim of the transition. It was no fault of Scott's, but it didn't work out."

Former Bournemouth team-mate Steve Cook added: " Bournemouth had the opportunity to sign him permanently (reportedly for £9m) but it didn't work out.

"He didn't let it stop him. First and foremost, he was a really good lad. He was energetic away from the football pitch and I think that character has helped take him to where he is now.

"He's a great example that not every journey is straightforward. You need setbacks to make you hungry and appreciate what you've got. He worked hard, listened, had a willingness to learn and wanted to prove people wrong."

Rogers' loan spell was cut short and he returned to academy football before an injury delayed his next move to Blackpool until the following January.

The move reunited Rogers with Appleton in the Championship, but the manager was sacked after only two weeks and replaced by Mick McCarthy.

Rogers made 20 appearances, both as a starter and substitute, scoring once as the Tangerines were relegated to League One after appointing a third manager in April.

"Unfortunately, he played one game against Watford and then I got sacked. That wasn't great for either of us," Appleton added.

"He'd been patient, I'd been patient while he recovered from his summer injury, we'd finally reconnected and then I was out of the building.

"I don't think he played as much as he would have liked after that, but he dealt with it professionally and in the right way."

Rogers says this period was "difficult" and tried not to compare himself to former team-mates who overtook him and got opportunities before him.

He even doubted whether he would make it but said his family and friends kept him grounded.

Notably, his "best friend in football", Cole Palmer, joined Chelsea for £42.5m having not needed a loan move to establish himself at Manchester City . At the same time, Rogers joined Middlesbrough for just £1m.

A run of five goals and three assists during Middlesbrough's six-game run to the Carabao Cup semi-finals alerted Aston Villa , where several of Rogers' former West Brom coaches were working in senior academy roles, to make an initial £8m move in the winter window.

By then, however, his close friend Palmer had already broken into the England squad through regular goals and assists for Chelsea .

"Morgan is a great example that careers aren't always a straight line," Appleton explained.

From a £9m prospect to a £1m gamble and eventually a £117m Chelsea signing, his story is a reminder that some of the best footballers need to overcome setbacks from a young age.

articles.title: Mariano, como una estrella del rock en República Dominicana: a besos con una fan
articles.standfirst: El delantero del Alavés fue sorprendido por una aficionada que se acercó para pedirle una foto
articles.summary: El delantero del Alavés fue sorprendido por una aficionada que se acercó para pedirle una foto
articles.body: Mariano Díaz se ha convertido en uno de los grandes protagonistas durante este parón internacional. El delantero de la República Dominicana está viviendo una etapa especialmente cercana con los aficionados de la selección caribeña, donde es una de las grandes figuras y con la que ha anotado dos dianas en esta ventana. El último episodio se produjo después del encuentro de la Nations League frente a Haití el pasado viernes. El resultado fue especialmente duro para los del delantero del Alavés, que terminaron goleados 1-4, pero la atención se desplazó rápidamente hacia lo ocurrido en los alrededores del estadio una vez terminado el partido. Un episodio que se ha viralizado ahora, días después del encuentro. A la salida, numerosos seguidores aguardaban al futbolista para conseguir una fotografía o simplemente saludarle. Mariano no dudó en detenerse y atender a los aficionados, entre los que había varios luciendo camisetas con su nombre. En medio de ese ambiente, una seguidora protagonizó una situación inesperada. Mientras posaban para una foto, la mujer fue acercándose progresivamente al jugador hasta terminar dándole un beso por sorpresa. Mariano reaccionó con evidente desconcierto ante la escena, aunque el momento acabó entre risas. La aficionada volvió a aproximarse y, esta vez, el delantero correspondió al gesto antes de continuar atendiendo a los demás seguidores.

articles.title: Nations League: How Northern Ireland built best defensive record in competition
articles.summary: With three clean sheets from three games in Uefa Nations League Group B2, Northern Ireland are the only team in this year's competition yet to concede a goal.
articles.body:
Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One NI, BBC Three, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary available online.

When Switzerland equalised in the 11th minute of their eventual 2-1 win over Slovenia on Saturday, there was just one team left in the 2026-27 Uefa Nations League yet to concede a goal - Northern Ireland.

Michael O'Neill's side have kept three consecutive clean sheets upon their return to the second tier of the competition, beating Georgia and Ukraine to nil with a scoreless stalemate against Hungary in between during this window.

Indeed, across this campaign and the 2024-25 edition when Northern Ireland played in League C, they have kept seven clean sheets in their past nine Nations League games, conceding just three goals in the process.

Should they manage to keep Georgia out again in Belfast on Monday night, it will be the side's longest run of clean sheets in nine years.

They did live somewhat dangerously in the reverse fixture in Tbilisi, with goalkeeper Pierce Charles saving a penalty from Paris St-Germain forward Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in a player of the match performance.

Despite the absence of Daniel Ballard and Conor Bradley through injury, the Queens Park Rangers loanee has had precious little to do in the two games since, however.

Hungary had their only shot on target in injury time at Windsor Park last week, while the side's record goalscorer David Healy described the stopper's two saves in the 3-0 victory against Ukraine as "ones for the camera".

"I think the clean sheets are a real plus for us and we want to maintain that because history tells us that Northern Ireland are never the highest scoring team," said O'Neill.

"If you look at the xG [Expected Goals] in the games, people have different opinions on that, but the xG for the opposition has been low and that means we've got a good defensive structure.

"It means our young defenders are coping with the game at this level, but it also means that we defend well as a team and the best teams do that."

NI team will 'have bumps along the road' - O'Neill

Who has 'no ceiling' as Northern Ireland shine in Nations League?

'Different' Morrison gives NI new option

Always evident in an effective O'Neill team is a desire to work hard off the ball. If Isaac Price, who scored his 11th international goal against Ukraine, is the closest thing the side have to a flair player, the West Bromwich Albion attacker still covers plenty of ground going the other way.

"You watch PSG, and their willingness to defend and to run, is a great example," added O'Neill.

"We have that ability to run when we lose the ball. We've got great recovery runners in our team, and that's a big reason why teams have found it difficult against us."

Already in this extended international window, O'Neill has talked of what he perceives as a "snobbery" about his team's style of play.

Comments made by then Germany boss Julian Nagelsmann last October were branded "disrespectful" by former Northern Ireland defender Stephen Craigan at the time, while opposition managers have frequently used words such as direct or physical in the months since.

Against Ukraine on Friday, Northern Ireland had 27.2% possession, according to Opta the lowest recorded in Nations League history for a win by more than one goal.

"We see some of the best teams play with very little possession as well. Sometimes you have teams who have a lot of possession but struggle to do anything with it," said O'Neill.

"You can control the game without the ball as much as with the ball."

Northern Ireland's long-ball statistics can be skewed somewhat by the fact that goalkeeper Pierce Charles possesses such a fantastic range of passing, and O'Neill cited his side's second goal against Ukraine as an example of the football his side can play.

"The quality of our play shouldn't be underestimated," he said.

"Our second goal against Ukraine, that's as good a goal as you'll see. The number of passes and how we worked the ball the full length of the pitch, the cross and the header.

"If you said 'would you love 60% possession?' then of course we would, but at this minute in time, that's an area to improve on.

"People have opinions, but really the only opinion that counts to me is that of the players and the belief that the players have."

On the evidence of recent results, that is no area of concern and Northern Ireland's defensive solidity is not just confined to the Nations League.

In all competitions they have kept eight clean sheets from their past 10 games at home and on Monday night Georgia will look to become the first visitors to Belfast to score more than once since Cyprus in June 2022.

"I think over the last three or four years, we've played the same system and I think boys are getting more comfortable and they understand their jobs," said Sunderland defender Trai Hume.

"That's not just the starting XI, it's the boys that come into the team who understand what they have to do too. On and off the ball you understand where you have to be on the pitch and, when you understand that, it makes the game a lot easier.

"Once you understand your role in the system, that's when you can start to express yourself and I think you're starting to see that."

articles.title: ¿Cómo cambia el patrocinio en el Big 5 del fútbol europeo? Apuestas, cripto y nuevos activos
articles.standfirst: El 93% de los fans prefiere las experiencias presenciales a las digitales y el 71% considera que los programas de fidelización se parecen demasiado entre sí
articles.summary: El 93% de los fans prefiere las experiencias presenciales a las digitales y el 71% considera que los programas de fidelización se parecen demasiado entre sí
articles.body: El mercado europeo de patrocinio sigue al alza, pero el reparto de activos y los sectores que ocupan los espacios de mayor visibilidad se transforman. Las cinco grandes ligas de fútbol -Premier League, LaLiga, Bundesliga, Serie A y Ligue 1- suman 2.488 contratos de patrocinio repartidos entre 1.784 marcas en 2026-2027, según la última edición de Big-5 Sponsor Landscape 2026. En términos interanuales, supone un 5% más de acuerdos y un 7% más de marcas. El estudio, elaborado en exclusiva por Intelligence 2P para todos los partners de la unidad de estrategia e inteligencia de mercado de 2Playbook, desglosa el patrocinio deportivo de los clubes de las cinco grandes ligas de fútbol de Europa. En juego, un negocio comercial que este año superará los 7.000 millones de euros entre los 96 clubes. La fotografía agregada confirma a las casas de apuestas, el sector financiero, la automoción, la tecnología y el retail deportivo como las categorías con mayor presencia comercial. Sin embargo, los límites a la visibilidad de operadores de juego en todos o algunos activos de la equipación - dependiendo del país - está modificando el reparto de los principales espacios de las camisetas, especialmente en aquellos mercados donde se han limitado sus espacios de exposición. El principal movimiento se produce en la manga de las camisetas, que ha ganado protagonismo para las compañías de apuestas y las firmas de criptomonedas. Bet365 aparece como la marca más activa en este activo. En paralelo, las entidades financieras y las compañías tecnológicas han ganado peso en el frontal, tradicionalmente reservado a las categorías con mayor capacidad de inversión. La dimensión internacional del Big-5 también explica la elevada concentración de algunas marcas. Coca-Cola suma 44 acuerdos y se sitúa como la compañía con mayor presencia transversal entre las cinco competiciones. Le siguen EA Sports, con 19 patrocinios, y Socios.com, con 18. En España, CaixaBank destaca como la única marca que supera los diez acuerdos dentro de una misma competición, en este caso LaLiga EA Sports. El patrocinio técnico presenta una estructura diferente, con 19 marcas activas entre las cinco grandes ligas. Sólo siete de ellas trabajan con un único club, entre las que están Austral o Kelme. En las antípodas están firmas con más presupuesto, con un claro protagonismo de Adidas, que alcanza una cuota del 26% del mercado del Big-5, después de incorporar tres clubes más en la última campaña. Nike ocupa la segunda posición, con un 14%, seguida de Puma, con un 11%, Macron, con un 8%, y Joma, con un 7%. Esta última se incorpora, junto a Adidas, Nike y Puma, al grupo de marcas presentes en las cinco grandes ligas. La duración de los contratos también evidencia diferencias entre mercados. LaLiga EA Sports registra la mayor estabilidad contractual en el patrocinio técnico, con una duración media de 11,5 temporadas por acuerdo. En España, la estructura comercial de los equipos de la Primera División española muestra también es estable. Esta temporada el 80% de los patrocinadores principales mantiene su acuerdo, mientras que la regulación ha limitado la exposición de las casas de apuestas respecto a otros mercados europeos. De los veinte clubes, 19 tienen ocupado el frontal de la camiseta, con el Sevilla FC como excepción. La tasa de penetración de la venta comercial de la manga de la camiseta es del 75%. El valor económico de la camiseta española, no obstante, está muy condicionado por los tres grandes clubes. El precio medio del frontal se sitúa en 12,3 millones de euros, aunque la cifra cae hasta aproximadamente 2 millones si se excluyen Real Madrid, FC Barcelona y Atlético de Madrid. En el patrocinio técnico, el promedio alcanza los 14,6 millones de euros. Pasando al patrocinio técnico de los clubes de LaLiga, el mercado está atomizado. Hummel, Joma, Macron y Nike alcanzan cada una un 15% de cuota, mientras que Adidas se queda en el 10%. Entre los principales patrocinadores de los clubes aparecen Kutxabank, Spotify, Riyadh Air, Estrella Galicia, Digi y TM Grupo Inmobiliario, mientras que EA Sports ejerce como Naming Sponsor de la competición. La fotografía cambia de forma sustancial al cruzar el mercado español con la Premier League. La competición inglesa incrementa un 8% los ingresos agregados procedentes de sus patrocinadores principales para 2026-2027, ampliando la distancia económica respecto al resto de grandes ligas europeas. El main & training Sponsor de la Premier alcanza un precio medio de 34,1 millones de euros, mientras que el patrocinio técnico se sitúa en 40,6 millones. La diferencia frente a LaLiga no sólo responde al tamaño de las audiencias internacionales de la competición inglesa, sino también a la capacidad de sus clubes para monetizar activos comerciales dentro de un ecosistema con una mayor escala global. Es más, la entrada en vigor de la prohibición de las casas de apuestas en el frontal de las camisetas a partir de 2026-2027 ha acelerado la reorganización del mercado inglés. Estas compañías han desplazado parte de su presencia hacia la manga y la ropa de entrenamiento, mientras que empresas financieras y tecnológicas han ocupado el frontal. El resultado es un incremento del valor comercial de la manga y una mayor competencia por los espacios de máxima visibilidad. El contraste también se reproduce en el patrocinio técnico. Adidas alcanza una cuota del 38% en la Premier League, muy por delante de Nike y Hummel, ambas con un 14%. Frente a la mayor fragmentación que presenta LaLiga, el mercado inglés concentra así una parte sustancial de sus acuerdos en las principales marcas internacionales de equipamiento. Por su parte, la Bundesliga destaca por la estabilidad de su modelo comercial y por el peso del tejido empresarial alemán. Los patrocinadores principales mantienen una vinculación media de 10,9 años, la duración más larga del Big-5, mientras 15 de los 18 clubes explotan los naming rights de sus estadios. Además, todos tienen vendidos tanto el paquete de patrocinio principal y de la ropa de entren, con un valor medio de 17,3 millones de euros, como el patrocinio técnico, que alcanza 12,4 millones. Adidas lidera este último mercado con un 32% de cuota. Entre los acuerdos de mayor valor destacan los 65 millones anuales de T-Mobile con el Bayern, los 35 millones de Red Bull con el Leipzig y los 30 millones de Vodafone con el Dortmund. La Serie A presenta un mercado más atomizado y en transformación, con 12 marcas distintas de equipamiento y un valor medio de 9,8 millones para el main & training y 8,6 millones para el patrocinio técnico. Adidas y Puma lideran con un 19% cada una, mientras los clubes exploran nuevos activos como parches adicionales y la trasera de la camiseta. En la Ligue 1, el valor cae hasta 5,5 millones de media de valor del patrocinio principal y de la ropa de entreno y 3,5 millones en el patrocinio técnico, en un mercado condicionado por la menor proyección internacional de la competición y la enorme distancia entre el PSG y el resto. Adidas también lidera el equipamiento, con un 32% de los equipos, mientras McDonald's da nombre a la liga y Qatar Airways mantiene uno de los principales acuerdos de clubes con el PSG.

articles.title: Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw
articles.summary: Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem
articles.body:
The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics , with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport : "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment .

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos .

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

articles.title: Proença, presidente de la Federación de Portugal, rompe su silencio con el caso Cristiano: "Fue un malentendido"
articles.standfirst: Habló sobre la polémica que rodea al capitán, a quien Jorge Jesus le abrió las puertas, y le garantizó que regresará para la próxima concentración si así lo desea.
articles.summary: Habló sobre la polémica que rodea al capitán, a quien Jorge Jesus le abrió las puertas, y le garantizó que regresará para la próxima concentración si así lo desea.
articles.body: Pedro Proença, presidente de la Federación Portuguesa de Fútbol, ha roto su silencio sobre la polémica entre Cristiano Ronaldo y Jorge Jesus. El dirigente ha calificado lo sucedido de "malentendido" y ha dejado claro que el delantero seguirá contando para Portugal mientras el seleccionador considere que está en condiciones. "Esas explicaciones no las voy a dar. Son conversaciones absolutamente normales entre entrenadores y jugadores. Es un área técnica y el presidente de la Federación no se mete en estas cuestiones", explicó Proença tras la victoria ante Noruega. El presidente de la FPF sí quiso reivindicar la figura de Cristiano Ronaldo y su importancia para el fútbol portugués. "Estamos hablando del mejor jugador de todos los tiempos, de un jugador que lleva más de dos décadas dándolo todo por el fútbol portugués. Cristiano Ronaldo representa hoy el mayor símbolo portugués. Tenemos que rendirle pleitesía", aseguró. Proença también descartó que la presencia de Ronaldo en la selección tenga que ver únicamente con su estatus. "Está en la Selección Nacional por méritos deportivos propios, y eso es absolutamente indiscutible. Siempre formará parte de este grupo de trabajo mientras esté técnicamente capacitado. Cristiano lo sabe, sabe que esa es la sensación. Sobre este tema en concreto, permítanme decir que nos enfrentamos a un malentendido que debe resolverse internamente", señaló. El dirigente portugués considera que el desencuentro debe resolverse internamente y confía en que las partes puedan reconducir la situación antes de la próxima convocatoria. "Era importante haber finalizado estos cuatro partidos con tranquilidad, porque el aspecto deportivo fue lo que nos guio. Tendremos tiempo y sosiego para sentarnos todos juntos y aclarar este malentendido. Reitero: Cristiano Ronaldo forma parte de nuestra historia y siempre estará aquí si el entrenador lo necesita", sentenció Proença. "La FPF, con calma, resuelve las situaciones internamente. Reitero: afortunadamente, existe una relación muy sólida entre Ronaldo y Jesús, soy testigo de ello, porque si no fuera así... seamos claros, quizás Ronaldo ya habría abandonado la Selección. No lo hace por esta relación y por el respeto que le tiene. Todo lo que ocurra en los próximos días serán momentos de tranquilidad, conversación, debate, y lo que queremos es que en noviembre podamos estar todos de vuelta con nuestra Selección", concluyó.

articles.title: Carreira, Álvaro Núñez y Aleix Febas vuelven a Elche
articles.standfirst: Los tres rindieron a muy buen nivel en el próximo rival céltico
articles.summary: Los tres rindieron a muy buen nivel en el próximo rival céltico
articles.body: El partido del próximo domingo en Elche, con el que los célticos reanudan su participación liguera, será especial para tres futbolistas del cuadro vigués. Sergio Carreira, Álvaro Núñez y Aleix Febas se reencuentran ante un equipo en el que ofrecieron muy buen rendimiento. Sergio Carreira vivió en Elche su tercera cesión, antes de quedarse definitivamente en la primera plantilla céltica hace ya más de dos años. El vigués, imprescindible para Claudio Giráldez, disputó 23 encuentros oficiales en el conjunto ilicitano, que entonces militaba en la Segunda división. Álvaro Núñez abandonó el Elche en el pasado mercado invernal. Era indiscutible en el equipo, en el año y medio que allí estuvo y en los que disputó 59 encuentros oficiales, marcando 2 goles. Ahora vive su mejor momento en el Celta, desde que llegase hace ocho meses. Mientras, Aleix Febas se verá por primera vez las caras ante el que fue su equipo hasta el pasado verano. Recuperado de las molestias físicas que ha sufrido en el arranque de esta temporada, el mediocampista fue indiscutible los tres años que jugó en Elche y en los que sumó 117 partidos oficiales en los que hizo 4 goles.

articles.title: Nuevo conflicto entre Israel e Irlanda: del "odio" y el racismo a los escupitajos
articles.standfirst: El segundo partido de la Nations Cup entre Irlanda e Israel también terminó con incidentes
articles.summary: El segundo partido de la Nations Cup entre Irlanda e Israel también terminó con incidentes
articles.body: Heimir Hallgrimsson, seleccionador de la República de Irlanda, declaró que sintió que Israel intentaba "intimidar" a su equipo, en medio de acusaciones de escupitajos durante el tenso partido que terminó 1-1 en la Nations League. Los jugadores de la República de Irlanda se han visto sometidos a constantes peticiones para que se retiren de los partidos debido a la guerra en curso entre Israel y Gaza. La campaña 'Stop The Game', organizada por el grupo de presión 'Irish Sport for Palestine', llevó a cabo protestas antes y durante el partido del jueves contra Austria en Dublín. Los equipos no cumplieron con los protocolos previos al partido en ninguno de los dos encuentros, y los jugadores irlandeses inclinaron la cabeza durante la interpretación del himno nacional de Israel. "Obviamente, nos odian y nosotros no les tenemos cariño. Tenemos un país diez veces mejor que el suyo", declaró Manor Solomon, capitán de Israel. 'Irish Times' publica que ambos equipos se encararon en el descanso del partido, que se jugó a puerta cerrada en Serbia. Damien Doyle, preparador físico de Irlanda, denunció que un jugador israelí le había escupido. En las imágenes de televisión se escucha una voz diciendo "me ha escupido" mientras los jugadores se dirigían al túnel de vestuarios del TSC Arena. Hallgrimsson le explicó a 'Off The Ball' al ser preguntado por el incidente que "no quiero entrar en eso, pero la situación ha sido así en estos dos partidos. Hay tensión, hay muchas emociones". "Fue una acusación de escupir a alguien, pero yo no lo vi. No, no queremos hablar de esto. Se revisará, probablemente como todo lo demás que ha ocurrido entre ambos equipos", apuntó. Heimir Hallgrimsson denunció sobre la selección de Israel que "sentí que intentaban intimidarnos desde el pitido inicial, pero reconozco el mérito de los jugadores por mantener la calma. Podría haber sido un partido lleno de tarjetas amarillas y rojas, pero mantuvimos la compostura; los jugadores estuvieron serenos y supieron controlar sus emociones". Al preguntársele por el incidente del descanso, el seleccionador de Israel, Ran Ben-Shimon, afirmó que "no vio nada". La BBC informa que las tensiones entre ambas partes se agudizaron el sábado, cuando la rueda de prensa previa al partido de la selección de la República de Irlanda concluyó abruptamente después de que Hallgrimsson recibiera lo que más tarde calificó como un "ataque verbal" por parte de periodistas israelíes. Un periodista israelí preguntó a Hallgrimsson sobre presuntos actos racistas por parte de jugadores irlandeses durante el partido disputado la semana pasada en Hungría, que la República de Irlanda ganó por 3-0. El periodista acusó al delantero irlandés Adam Idah de haber llamado "monos" a los jugadores israelíes durante el primer partido. La rueda de prensa fue dada por terminada en ese momento por Kieran Crowley, responsable de comunicación de la Asociación de Fútbol de Irlanda (FAI), quien calificó dichas acusaciones de "totalmente falsas" a medida que el ambiente se tensaba. Esto ocurrió tras conocerse que la FAI está investigando si el delantero de la República de Irlanda, Adam Idah, sufrió insultos racistas por parte de aficionados israelíes durante el primer partido, celebrado en Debrecen. Jayson Molumby habló con los árbitros durante el encuentro para pedirles que prestaran atención a lo que él consideraba cánticos ofensivos provenientes de un pequeño grupo de aficionados israelíes presentes en el estadio. "No había nada personal contra Molumby... Vamos, vamos. Nosotros no hacemos eso. Simplemente no lo hacemos; no somos esa clase de hombres", declaró Ben-Shimon defendiendo el comportamiento de los jugadores de Israel. El seleccionador de Israel insistió en que "es muy difícil que nos crean, pero jamás le pediría a un jugador que juegue de forma agresiva contra él (un rival). A veces no me gusta eso, pero les digo a mis jugadores que, en ocasiones, esa es la mejor manera de practicar el fútbol más limpio posible, sin dejar de ser agresivos". "Nunca les digo que insulten a nadie. Esa no es nuestra forma de actuar; somos seres humanos", subrayó.

articles.title: Alex Scott: Bournemouth unhappy after midfielder injured on England duty
articles.summary: Bournemouth are unhappy with the way they believe England handled the injury to Alex Scott - which means he could now be out for up to eight weeks.
articles.body:
Bournemouth are unhappy with the way they believe England handled the injury to midfielder Alex Scott - which means he could now be out for up to eight weeks.

Scott has withdrawn from the England squad to face the Czech Republic in the Nations League on Tuesday with a thigh injury.

He felt the issue prior to Saturday's 7-0 win over Croatia, but played 70 minutes in central midfield alongside Elliot Anderson before being substituted.

England coach Thomas Tuchel described Scott's injury as "a strange one" in his Monday news conference.

"I'm very sad about it. He trained in full before Croatia, did extra work after the training sessions, we knew he was in treatment but there were only green lights from him and the medics," said Tuchel.

"When we were aware there was slight discomfort during the match and asked if he wanted to come off he said no. After the match, he said he could have played 90 minutes and didn't feel an injury.

"Even before the scan he didn't feel injured so it's a strange one. There was zero risk taken from our side."

However, according to sources, there is frustration at Bournemouth about how England have handled their midfielder, given they knew he was nursing the thigh issue.

The 23-year-old is now set to be out for six to eight weeks with the quadriceps issue.

Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa has also been ruled out of the fixture at Wembley as a precautionary measure, with the 28-year-old to return to the Premier League champions for treatment on an injury.

Tuchel said that Konsa's issues were "nothing major but not worth the risk taking" after the centre-back first missed the match with the Czech Republic in Prague on 29 September and then sustained an injury against Croatia.

"Ezri felt discomfort when he came into camp, played with it against Spain and it got a bit worse so he stayed in camp and tried everything for the match against the Czech Republic and it came too soon," Tuchel added.

"Unfortunately, he got another hit on the quad and that caused a light trauma and we decided not to let him play through this pain, so he left camp to get treatment for both his issues now."

Scott is now likely to be absent for the nine games Bournemouth are due to play between 10 October and 8 November.

Alongside their weekend Premier League commitments, they will play on Wednesday or Thursday for four consecutive weeks, facing Sturm Graz, AC Milan and Sparta Prague in the Europa League and Aston Villa in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

Scott made his England debut in the 2-0 win over the Czech Republic, before his full debut four days later, after which Tuchel was effusive with his praise.

"First start and what a start, what a performance," said Tuchel. "He is so smooth on the ball, his decision making is at the highest level.

"He plays with so much confidence. He is so active, so confident. The work rate off the ball.

"He is just the complete package. He gave us a lot of mobility and a lot of variety and work rate in the centre of the pitch."

Scott joins French forward Eli Junior Kroupi on Bournemouth's injury list, with the 20-year-old still unavailable after sustaining a foot problem in pre-season.

The Cherries are 17th in the Premier League and are winless after five matches, drawing three times and losing twice.

Marco Rose's side defeated Lincoln to progress in the EFL Cup, and won 2-1 at La Liga side Real Sociedad on their European debut.

They return to Premier League action at Chelsea on Saturday (15:00 BST) and play Sunderland, Manchester United, Leeds and Ipswich prior to the November international break.

articles.title: La foto de Huijsen y Pitarch que está dando que hablar: una mano en el volante y la otra en el móvil
articles.standfirst: El centrocampista compartió en sus redes una instantánea que no ha pasado desapercibida
articles.summary: El centrocampista compartió en sus redes una instantánea que no ha pasado desapercibida
articles.body: Nuevo episodio que está dando que hablar en el Real Madrid. Si hace unas horas corrió como la pólvora el vídeo que subió Mbappé montando en bici -días después de las declaraciones de Mourinho en la que explicaba que un jugador profesional no debería hacer este tipo de actividad-, ahora ha sido una foto de Thiago Pitarch con Huijsen la que se está cargando de críticas. El joven centrocampista español, que ha sido llamado con la selección sub 20, compartió una foto en sus redes sociales dentro de un coche donde su compañero Dean Huijsen sostiene el teléfono móvil con una mano... y el volante con la otra. Una acción que no ha pasado desapercibida y que, a pesar de no quedar claro si el coche está en movimiento o no, ha multiplicado los comentarios negativos en redes sociales de numerosos aficionados del Real Madrid por lo que consideran una temeridad.

articles.title: "Mbappé está echando un pulso al Real Madrid"
articles.standfirst: Javier Tintó analiza la actuación del francés y revela la petición que hizo al club para que hicieran una campaña por su Balón de Oro
articles.summary: Javier Tintó analiza la actuación del francés y revela la petición que hizo al club para que hicieran una campaña por su Balón de Oro
articles.body: Nacho Palencia, Javier Tintó, Emilio Pérez de Rozas, Látigo Serrano, Ricardo Rosety y Alberto Santacruz han sido los tertulianos de este lunes en La Tribu, patrocinada por Sportium durante esta temportada para analizar la actualidad deportiva, marcada por el parón de selecciones y esas imágenes de Mbappé montando en bicicleta. "Es un jugador que solo piensa en sí mismo y que le da igual todo", comenzó diciendo Tintó. "Lo que me dicen es que la semana del derbi Mbappé pide al club un esfuerzo y que haga una campaña a favor de su Balón de Oro, que es lo que a él le interesa. El club no cede. Ya me cuadra la actitud de Mbappé ese derbi y es por eso, por ese enfado. Al parecer a Zidane también le pide ese esfuerzo y Zidane no puede hacerlo porque está también Dembélé", explicó el tertuliano sobre lo que está pasando con el futbolista del Real Madrid. Tintó también explicó lo que ha acontecido con Mbappé durante este parón. A partir de ahí lo que pasa es lamentable. Se lesiona, hay prensa que dice que evita el quirófano, llega al médico del Real Madrid y en 20 minutos le ven la rodilla y le dicen que no tiene nada. Se va a Francia de vacaciones, como ya os avisé, luego sale corriendo en la elíptica que se cree que somos tontos, no ha pasado por Valdebebas... Y ahora el colmo, que hay que ser torpe...", resumió. "Mbappé ni es torpe ni tonto, es un pulso al club. Todo es orquestado. Lo que pasa que él no sabe dónde está, no sabe cómo el Bernabéu se va a volcar. Me gusta que pase esto para que vean a quién quieren darle las llaves del Madrid y lo profesional que es", lanzó el colaborador de La Tribu, visiblemente molesto por todo lo que ha acontecido con el internacional francés.

El conjunto dirigido por Zinedine Zidane, que no pudo pasar del empate pese a la genialidad a balón parado de Michael Olise, buscará recuperar su versión más arolladora y hacer valer su caudal ofensivo en campo rival. Con la baja sensible en la retaguardia de Dayot Upamecano tras ser expulsado en la anterior jornada, el combinado galo intentará afinar la puntería en los últimos metros para sumar tres puntos clave en la lucha por el liderato de grupo. Por su parte, la selección de Bélgica llega a la cita impulsada por las buenas sensaciones transmitidas en su holgada victoria por 3-0 frente a Turquía. Bajo la dirección de Mark van Bommel, los 'Diablos Rojos' tiraron de efectividad ofensiva con el protagonismo anotador de Kevin De Bruyne y Romelu Lukaku para consolidarse en la zona alta de la tabla. Sin embargo, el cuadro visitante afronta este exigente desplazamiento con importantes contratiempos en la medular debido a las ausencias confirmadas del propio De Bruyne y Youri Tielemans, por lo que necesitará un ejercicio de máxima disciplina colectiva para asaltar el feudo francés. articles.title: Bellingham, con las islas a sus pies: "Puede llegar a convertirse en uno de los mejores de todos los tiempos"
articles.standfirst: Roy Keane se deshace en elogios hacia el de Birmingham
articles.summary: Roy Keane se deshace en elogios hacia el de Birmingham
articles.body: No baja el nivel. Después de un Mundial estratosférico en el que lideró a Inglaterra al tercer puesto, Jude Bellingham mantiene su 'prime' con los 'Three Lions'. Y Reino Unido, se lo reconoce. No solo aficionados o analistas ingleses; también Roy Keane, desde Irlanda, elogia al centrocampista de Birmingham. "Bellingham puede llegar a convertirse en uno de los mejores jugadores de todos los tiempos", avanza, directamente, el histórico futbolista irlandés en 'ITV'. Jude, que anotó un gol y firmó tres asistencias en el histórico 0-7 de Rijeka sobre Croacia, también asistió en la derrota ante España en Wembley. "Su actitud con la selección inglesa últimamente... lo he elogiado por ser fantástico con el balón, pero lo que hace sin él es lo que motiva a todos estos jugadores. Si tienes en tu equipo a un jugador tan bueno, que es increíble con el balón y juega en el Real Madrid y hace cosas brillantes, pero sobre todo su entrega sin balón, eso inspirará a todos los demás jugadores", prosigue un Roy Keane que identifica a Bellingham como un líder de la selección de Tuchel. Bellingham, mientras, y a falta del partido ante República Checa en esta Nations League, se ha convertido en el primer centrocampista inglés en participar de forma directa en cuatro goles en un partido (0-7 sobre Croacia) desde David Platt ante San Marino... ¡en 1993!. Inglaterra cerrará este parón de selecciones este martes ante la República Checa, en casa. Un partido decisivo para cerrar virtualmente la clasificación a los cuartos de final de la Nations y poder seguir aspirando al primer puesto que, ahora mismo, defiende España.

articles.title: Reporter notebook: Why England's 7-0 victory in Croatia is angrifying for every fan
articles.summary: England put seven past Croatia in Rijeka in a sensational Nations League win that represents the best performance of the Thomas Tuchel era; Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored twice while Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Morgan Rogers were also on target for the Three Lions
articles.body:
When it came, for the 100 fans watching in the stadium and the millions at home, it was thrilling, inspiring and fulfilling.

But it was also angrifying, for every England supporter.

Because that is the England we want to see in the biggest games at the key moments in major tournaments. The sort of performance that beats the best opposition in the world when it really matters, and leads us to the holy grail of a shiny trophy. That probably sounds churlish. Because this was an important game, a competitive game.

Croatia are a top footballing nation, ranked 14th in the FIFA world rankings, and England humbled them in their own backyard. And maybe that performance is an important milestone, a blueprint to show how England can and should play on the international stage, and towards the players truly believing they can beat the world's best.

But let's not forget that exactly a week before, England had played the world's best. And lost. With another "nearly" performance against Spain, the reigning World and European champions.

What the victory in Rijeka has surely done is cast the despair and anger at the manner of England's World Cup exit into the darkest corners of the supporters' memories. The hangover has been eased, and that is important for the belief in Thomas Tuchel going forward. Because make no mistake, at the start of this extended international break, the England head coach was under real pressure.

The tactical decisions taken to go hyper-defensive in the latter stages of the World Cup semi-final against Argentina was met with fury from England fans - and some England players. That led to doubts - credible doubts - about Tuchel's future. In the early parts of this international camp, he looked moody, distracted, brooding. He was clearly angered by the pesky media who kept dragging up issues around that defeat to Argentina two months earlier in Atlanta.

By contrast, what we saw in the tiny Rijeka Stadium on the edge of the Adriatic Sea was the epitome of how Tuchel wants his team to play. Pace, power, quick passing, forward passing, high pressing, dynamic movement, ruthless finishing. That is surely what the German coach means when he says he wants his England to play in "the Premier League way".

England's front four were irresistible. Harry Kane told me after the game that they now have a unique understanding which leads to new levels of "fluidity", where they can all switch positions, fill in for one another right across the pitch, and by doing so pull an opponent's defence to pieces. It is reminiscent of the 'Total Football' Johan Cruyff's Netherlands side created in the 1970s. Tuchel would call those special "connections" - that innate understanding between individual players that pushes them to new heights of performance. He has been calling for it to become second nature for England's "core group of senior players" ever since he took the top job.

While it is gladdening and heartening to see England play like this, there are, however, still some provisos. Some "Yeah, but…" sentiments.

Firstly, this is clearly one of the worst incarnations of the recently great Croatian football sides. Slaven Bilic knows he has his work cut out to replace the generational talent that is Luka Modric who is now, finally, fading at 41 years old, and Ivan Perisic who was horribly exposed by Bukayo Saka, and who is only four years Modric's junior. Technically and positionally, Croatia were very poor. Physically, they were fragile. Defensively, they were woeful.

Of course, England's brilliance helped expose those failures. But we should remember that England teams often save their best performances for the autumn, in the early part of the season, when players are at their freshest and temperatures have cooled. It is no coincidence that England's players often struggle in summer tournaments, with sweltering conditions and the latent exhaustion that comes to them all at the end of an unforgiving Premier League season.

And so that leads us to ask the difficult question whether what we saw in Rijeka, that 'Premier League-style masterclass', is only achievable for England teams outside major tournaments. Kane admitted after the Euros in Germany in 2024 what he repeated after the World Cup in the US in the summer: that in neither of those competitions had England ever hit the heights they are capable of. The heights we have now seen in full technicolour in the third round of the Nations League.

We must hope, of course, that England are still evolving, still developing, still growing. Certainly, Gordon, Bellingham, Anderson and - the newly-capped smooth technician that is Alex Scott - will only improve in the years to come. And maybe we will look back at this game in Croatia as a key moment in England's progression, when the players proved to themselves, and the world, that they are capable of taking the next step. The crucial step, that ends with their name engraved on a trophy.

But until they can replicate what we have just watched, on the biggest stage against the biggest opponents, we will all still wonder. And worry.

articles.title: La atrevida comparación de Santi Denia: "Gordon está al mismo nivel que Lamine Yamal"
articles.standfirst: El seleccionador de la República Checa sorprendió elogiando al fichaje del Barcelona antes de volver a medirse a Inglaterra
articles.summary: El seleccionador de la República Checa sorprendió elogiando al fichaje del Barcelona antes de volver a medirse a Inglaterra
articles.body: La República Checa, rival de España el pasado sábado en la tercera jornada de la UEFA Nations League, se volverá a medir este martes (20:45 horas) a la Inglaterra de Thomas Tuchel. Y en la rueda de prensa previa al encuentro, el técnico español Santi Denia no ha dudado en elogiar a los 'Three Lions'. "Ha habido muchas finales, muchos momentos con Inglaterra. Llegué a la federación española en 2010 y la Federación Inglesa de Fútbol es la que más ha crecido. Ganaron una Eurocopa Sub-17, un Mundial Sub-17 en India, una Eurocopa Sub-21... porque han creído en invertir en la juventud y han apoyado su desarrollo. Les brindas oportunidades y experiencias que luego se reflejan en la selección absoluta. La Federación Inglesa lo vio antes que el resto", comenzó diciendo. Entre los jugadores que Denia veía a menudo está Anthony Gordon, fichaje del Barcelona este verano. Al ser preguntado por él, Denia sorprendió con el elogio hacia el delantero, que días atrás dijo que Inglaterra no debía centrarse en imitar el juego de España "¿Gordon? ¡Qué jugador!", respondió Denia. "¡Qué futbolista, Dios mío! Está al mismo nivel que… no sé, iba a decir Lamine. Joven, atrevido, en el uno contra uno, rápido... Y qué gran trabajo ha hecho el fútbol inglés formando jugadores como él", añadió. Centrándose puramente en las palabras del jugador azulgrana sobre los estilos de juego de ambas selecciones, Denia fue claro: "Mira, cada país tiene su esencia, hay que respetarla y aceptarla. Tampoco se puede cambiar de la noche a la mañana; el éxito no es inmediato, es un proceso. Se cometerán errores, pero hay que tener claro a dónde se va. En 15 años con las inferiores nos desarrollamos, evolucionamos, nos adaptamos. Mira lo que hacen otras federaciones... Eso no es copiar, es aprender", reflexionó. La comparecencia acabó con un nuevo elogio hacia Inglaterra. "Inglaterra es muy, muy buena; está a un paso de la final del Mundial. Defiendo mucho a la Federación Inglesa, está entre las dos o tres mejores selecciones del mundo, siempre ahí. La Federación lo vio, invirtió, y les animo a que sigan haciéndolo: en jugadores jóvenes y en la formación de técnicos", finalizó.
